Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The issue reported describes that multiple iterators obtained from the same CSVParser instance share the same underlying lexer state. Each call to iterator() creates a new Iterator referencing the shared parser state. The Iterator implementation caches the next record in a current field to support hasNext() peeking without advancing. However, this only works correctly within a single Iterator's lifecycle.

Inspecting CSVParser.iterator() reveals that each call creates a fresh Iterator object with a null current record cache. When hasNext() is called on this new Iterator, it tries to fetch the next record by invoking CSVParser.nextRecord(), which advances the underlying lexer's position and consumes a record. Thus the state moves forward.

In the failing test, the first iterator partially consumes rows and breaks early. The second iterator, created anew, also calls hasNext() once (to peek) that triggers fetching the next record. Because the parser's lexer has already advanced, the record fetched by the second iterator at hasNext() is the next one in sequence, but it has been consumed and cached by the new iterator, unavailable to a previous iterator that was interrupted. This makes records "disappear" from the view of the iterators created subsequently.

This behavior differs from a usual expectation: new iterators should start iteration from the beginning or at the current logical position, but not consume unseen records prematurely on hasNext peeks.

The root cause is the shared mutable state between multiple iterators from the same CSVParser instance combined with the caching logic in hasNext(). The new iterator's first call to hasNext() reads from the shared parser and consumes the next record, breaking the outer sequential iteration logic expected by the test case.

Hence, "Some multi-iterator parsing peek sequences incorrectly consume elements" - repeated calls to CSVParser.iterator() cause new iterator objects sharing state. hasNext() calls on these new iterators consume tokens from the lexer's stream, causing records to be consumed prematurely and lost to subsequent iteration.

This diagnosis aligns with the test failure, as the test explicitly verifies that breaking and reacquiring iterators does not lose any records. The observed bug occurs exactly when invoking hasNext() on a freshly created iterator after another iterator was partially consumed and broken out of, matching the test setup and the bug summary.

Next, we should identify fixes restricting how multiple iterator instances share state or change how the peeking logic is implemented to avoid consuming elements on fresh iterator creation.
